title: Introduction to Vectors

findings.finding: The opening examples require signed, implicit and reordered vector components without an opening review of reading components.
findings.breakdown: Students must recognise the coefficient of −i as −1 and match components by basis symbol rather than printed order before substituting into the new formula.
findings.checked: The complete teaching contains no preceding topic or review. Both component-reading demands occur directly in the worked examples.
findings.assumptions: Component notation is prior learning from Vector Representation and Operations. Calculator availability is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before p3-definition-block add three short items: (a) Write 3i−4j as a column vector. Answer: (3,−4)ᵀ. (b) State the i and j components of 2j−3i. Answer: −3 and 2. (c) Write −i+6j as a column vector. Answer: (−1,6)ᵀ. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse identifying signed, implicit and reordered components before the dot-product examples.

findings.finding: Extend the existing calculation to expose how scaling one vector scales its dot product.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects scalar multiplication with the two component products.
findings.checked: The original equation gives x=−12 and u·v=24. Consequently (2u)·v=48 and (−u)·v=−24. Component calculation supplies the explanation using available methods.
findings.assumptions: Scalar multiplication is prior vector knowledge.

repair.proposal: Append to p4-q4: (b) Find (2u)·v. Answer: 48. (c) Find (−u)·v. Answer: −24. (d) Explain why doubling u doubles the dot product. Expected answer: both components of u double, so both component products and their sum double.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the original vectors to connect scalar multiplication and the dot product.

findings.finding: Hold both magnitudes fixed while varying the angle to expose the dot product's change through zero.
findings.breakdown: The run connects acute, right and obtuse angles with positive, zero and negative dot products.
findings.checked: For magnitudes 6 and 5, the proposed answers are 30, 15, 0, −15 and −30. The unpatterned answer is 28cos135°=−14√2. The existing exercise has no comparable run; p9 later provides a related investigation with unit vectors.
findings.assumptions: Exact special-angle cosine values are available from prior trigonometry.

repair.proposal: After p8-q1-b add: “Predict the sign before calculating.” For each of parts (c)–(g), use |a|=6 and |b|=5: (c) θ=0°, answer 30; (d) θ=60°, answer 15; (e) θ=90°, answer 0; (f) θ=120°, answer −15; (g) θ=180°, answer −30. Follow with (h) |a|=7, |b|=4, θ=135°, answer −14√2. Only the angle varies in the run.

findings.doneWhen: The added parts vary only the angle before an unpatterned application.

findings.finding: p17-q6 combines symbolic trigonometric displacements and an unscaffolded perpendicularity proof before the exercise's scaffolded proof of the same circle theorem.
findings.breakdown: The preceding numerical questions do not bridge forming two symbolic displacement vectors, expanding their dot product and recognising the trigonometric cancellation.
findings.checked: p12 supplies symbolic coordinate-proof experience, but not trigonometric coordinates. p24-q14 already separates displacement formation from the perpendicularity conclusion for the same circle theorem and supplies a suitable bridge.
findings.assumptions: Students know sin²θ+cos²θ=1 from prior trigonometry. Calculator availability is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Move p17-q6-root to immediately after p24-q14-root. Retain both questions: q14 first scaffolds the vector proof of the circle theorem; q6 then applies it independently using trigonometric coordinates.

findings.doneWhen: The scaffolded circle proof precedes the independent proof with trigonometric coordinates.

findings.finding: Reverse the existing rhombus argument to identify a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up reuses the diagonal expressions while reversing the given condition and conclusion.
findings.checked: For a nondegenerate parallelogram, perpendicular diagonals give 0=(a+b)·(a−b)=|a|²−|b|². Equal adjacent side lengths then establish a rhombus. This short generalisation uses the topic's notation and qualifies in Stage 6.

repair.proposal: Append to p22-q12: (f) Now suppose OACB is a parallelogram whose diagonals OC and BA are perpendicular. Use (a+b)·(a−b) to show that |a|=|b|. Expected answer: 0=|a|²−|b|², so |a|=|b|. (g) Identify OACB. Answer: a rhombus, because its adjacent sides have equal lengths.

findings.doneWhen: Students use the existing diagonal calculation to establish the converse.

findings.finding: Project the perpendicular component back onto b to connect decomposition with zero projection.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up makes students calculate what remains parallel to b after subtracting the perpendicular component.
findings.checked: Here w=(17/25)(3,−4), so w·b=0 and proj_b w=(0,0). Also a−w=(31/25)(4,3), whose projection onto b is itself. Both calculations use the taught projection formula.
findings.assumptions: b=(4,3) is nonzero; no additional methods are required.

repair.proposal: Label the existing task (a), then append: (b) Let w be your perpendicular component from part (a). Find proj_b w. Answer: (0,0). (c) Find proj_b(a−w). Answer: (31/25)(4,3).

findings.doneWhen: Students calculate the projections of both components of the existing decomposition.

protectedGroups.observation: The dot product falls from 1 through zero to -1 as the angle increases.
protectedGroups.invariant: Both magnitudes are 1 and one vector points right.

protectedGroups.observation: Reflecting a configuration across the horizontal vector preserves its dot product.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether the second vector lies above or below the first.
protectedGroups.invariant: The magnitudes and non-reflex angle within each pair.

protectedGroups.observation: With a fixed horizontal first vector, the dot product changes with the second vector's horizontal component.
protectedGroups.varies: The second vector's horizontal component, from 0 to 4.
protectedGroups.invariant: The first vector is (3,0) and the second vector's vertical component is 3.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing one arrow changes whether the marked angle qualifies.
protectedGroups.varies: The direction of the left vector.
protectedGroups.invariant: The segment arrangement and marked angle.

protectedGroups.observation: Angle size alone does not determine whether the diagram shows the angle between the vectors.
protectedGroups.varies: The direction of the right vector.
protectedGroups.invariant: The shallow V arrangement and marked obtuse sector.

protectedGroups.observation: The triangle midpoint relation becomes the building block for proving that a quadrilateral's midpoint polygon is a parallelogram.
protectedGroups.varies: One midpoint segment in a triangle becomes two opposite midpoint segments in a quadrilateral.
protectedGroups.invariant: Each midpoint segment is half the relevant diagonal vector.

protectedGroups.observation: Related diagonal expressions distinguish equal diagonal lengths from perpendicular diagonals and then reverse the rectangle implication.
protectedGroups.varies: The geometric assumptions and the dot-product expression used to reach the conclusion.
protectedGroups.invariant: Diagonal vectors are sums or differences of adjacent side vectors, and self-dot products represent squared lengths.

protectedGroups.observation: Projection keeps only the displacement in the requested axis direction, including its sign.
protectedGroups.varies: Vector direction and the requested horizontal or vertical component.
protectedGroups.invariant: Perpendicular projection onto the requested axis direction.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing projection order changes the receiving line and resulting vector; obtuse angles place the projection on a backwards extension.
protectedGroups.varies: Projection order within each pair, then the vector arrangement between pairs.
protectedGroups.invariant: The given vector pair within each adjacent pair and the perpendicular-foot construction.

protectedGroups.observation: Projection and rejection use the same decomposition whether the parallel component points forwards or backwards.
protectedGroups.varies: The sign of the parallel component.
protectedGroups.invariant: The perpendicular construction and original vector equals projection plus rejection.

protectedGroups.observation: Projection order matters even though the numerator dot product is unchanged.
protectedGroups.varies: The receiving vector within each pair.
protectedGroups.invariant: The two given vectors and their dot product.
